content: The Five-Year Global Strategic Plan to Improve Public Health Preparedness and Response (2018–2023) was introduced to enhance the capacities of both the World Health Organization (WHO) and its Member States. This plan focuses on implementing the International Health Regulations (IHR, 2005) through three key strategies: building and maintaining the core capacities required under the IHR, strengthening event management and compliance with IHR requirements, and measuring progress while promoting accountability. WHO plays a critical role in aligning this strategic plan with the Global Strategy for Influenza. Efforts by WHO and its partners to assist countries in developing influenza-related capacities contribute significantly to the first two pillars of this plan. In 2012, WHO’s Strategic Advisory Group of Experts (SAGE) on Immunization updated its recommendations for influenza vaccination, targeting specific populations such as pregnant women, healthcare workers, children aged 6–59 months, elderly individuals, and those with chronic conditions. While some countries have adopted universal vaccination policies for individuals over six months of age, the 2012 SAGE recommendations have helped nations prioritize key target groups based on national disease burden data. In December 2017, a new SAGE working group on influenza was established to review scientific evidence and programmatic considerations, assessing whether sufficient data exists to revise global policies on influenza vaccine use. The Global Action Plan for Influenza Vaccines (GAP), launched in 2006, was a ten-year strategy aimed at addressing global shortages and inequities in access to pandemic influenza vaccines. This was achieved through three approaches: increasing evidence-based seasonal vaccine use, expanding vaccine production capacity, and promoting research and development of more effective vaccines. GAP facilitated the transfer of influenza vaccine production technology to 14 lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), contributing to global vaccine production capacity. WHO developed the Public Health Research Agenda for Influenza in 2009 to generate evidence for strengthening public health guidance and actions against pandemic, zoonotic, and seasonal influenza. A 2013 progress review highlighted significant funding and advancements in addressing knowledge gaps, though further work was deemed necessary. Given the evolving nature of influenza viruses, WHO updated the research agenda in 2017 to focus on high-priority areas and unmet public health needs over the next 5–10 years. WHO collaborates with the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and the World Organisation for Animal Health (OIE) to promote the One Health approach, which emphasizes cross-sectoral coordination to address public health threats at the human-animal-ecosystem interface. The 2010 Tripartite Agreement outlined a collective strategy for these organizations to work together in supporting countries. In 2017, FAO, OIE, and WHO reaffirmed their commitment to preventing and controlling zoonotic influenza while maintaining momentum in this area. Following the 2013–2016 Ebola crisis, the WHO Health Emergencies Programme (WHE) was launched in July 2016 to address the full risk management cycle, including prevention, preparedness, response, and recovery. WHE leads and coordinates international responses to disease outbreaks and provides effective relief and recovery for affected populations. The program operates with a unified structure across WHO headquarters, regional offices, and country offices, encompassing one workforce, one budget, one accountability line, and standardized processes and benchmarks. During health emergencies, including influenza pandemics, WHE manages responses through the Incident Management System outlined in the WHO Emergency Response Framework. Influenza surveillance is essential for understanding the virus. Over the past decade, the Global Influenza Surveillance and Response System (GISRS) has been strengthened, with 130 Member States sharing influenza viruses with GISRS in 2017. However, some countries lack the capacity to detect novel influenza viruses, a critical component of IHR core capacities. Improvements in data and virus sharing are needed for accurate risk assessments of influenza viruses with pandemic potential. Enhanced systems to assess disease severity are also crucial for developing appropriate pandemic responses. Understanding the disease and economic burden of influenza is vital for countries to develop effective prevention, control, and preparedness policies. While most burden estimates come from high-income countries, additional studies in LMICs are needed to better understand geographical and risk-group-specific burdens. Regional and global collaboration can help pool data and extrapolate trends to address these gaps. To support pandemic preparedness, WHO has developed guidance on risk-based strategies for influenza preparedness and response, encouraging countries to create sustainable and resilient plans. A checklist published in 2018 assists countries in updating their plans. However, as of September 2018, many countries either lacked updated plans or had plans that were not publicly available. Pandemic preparedness planning should align with national health security efforts to maximize efficiency and utilize existing systems effectively. Non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs), such as social distancing in schools, workplaces, and events, are critical tools for limiting influenza transmission. During the 1918 pandemic, NPIs were the only available interventions, and historical evidence supports their effectiveness when implemented early and in layers. Since the 2009 pandemic, many countries have integrated NPIs into their national influenza preparedness plans, and contemporary studies continue to assess their effectiveness. Antiviral drugs and other treatments are essential for improving influenza prevention, control, and preparedness. However, global use of antivirals for seasonal influenza remains low, limiting current supplies and surge capacity. Antiviral drugs play a prominent role during pandemics, especially in the early months when vaccines are unavailable. Countries should include antivirals in their pandemic preparedness efforts, as they are feasible to stockpile. Resistance to antiviral drugs is a public health concern, and optimizing their use through new formulations, delivery routes, and combination therapies is imperative. Vaccines remain the most effective intervention for preventing influenza infection and reducing clinical severity. However, challenges in vaccine production persist, as most rely on embryonated eggs, a time-intensive process that may be compromised during a pandemic. Efforts are underway to develop alternative vaccine technologies, such as cell-based, recombinant, and adjuvanted vaccines, which offer stronger, broader, and longer-lasting protection. WHO has published preferred product characteristics to guide the development of next-generation influenza vaccines, emphasizing the need for vaccines suitable for LMIC settings. Seasonal influenza vaccination programs are critical for testing vaccine deployment systems annually. However, disparities in vaccine distribution and use remain significant, particularly in regions such as the Eastern Mediterranean, South-East Asia, and Africa. Addressing barriers to vaccine distribution, confidence, and uptake is essential for strengthening seasonal vaccination programs and pandemic preparedness.
